results.title: Global Impact of Tariffs on Supply Chains
results.content:
The impact of tariffs on supply chain costs is immediate and widespread. When tariffs rise, prices for steel, aluminum, resins, and plastics increase. These materials are essential for packaging production, so even small changes affect overall expenses. As costs grow, shipping and freight rates often climb as well. Supplier contracts may also need renegotiation to reflect higher import fees and compliance requirements. [...] For companies dependent on packaging products, tariffs represent a double challenge: rising raw material costs and increased duties on finished packaging imports. These shifts create a cascading effect across industries. Leaders navigating these changes often feel stuck between unpredictable expenses and the urgent need to stay competitive. [...] ### Consumer Electronics Complexity

Tariffs are increasing costs for key electronic components and protective packaging. Plastics, foams, and aluminum materials face higher import duties, straining supply chains. Manufacturers are having to adjust sourcing strategies to meet launch schedules and protect fragile products. These cost pressures make maintaining consistent quality and margins more challenging worldwide.

results.title: How Tariffs Impact Procurement and Supply Chains in 2026 | Ivalua
results.content:
Changing tariffs on imports from China and other regions targeting key sectors like automotive, technology, and consumer goods are creating ripples across multiple industries, affecting not just manufacturers but the entire supply chain network that depends on imported materials and components. [...] Understanding the full tariff impact on supply chain operations requires visibility into sourcing dependencies, cost structures, and regional supplier concentration.
 Supply Chain Complexity: Global supply chains are intricate, and a sudden hike in tariffs could disrupt longstanding supplier relationships, necessitating rapid shifts to new suppliers—often at a higher cost or lower reliability. [...] To effectively manage the impact of tariffs on supply chains, procurement risk management needs to go beyond a list of primary suppliers — teams must understand how their suppliers source materials, which suppliers are at risk, and where potential vulnerabilities lie in the extended supply chain. They must map their full supply chain.

These taxes are paid at the point of entry into the United States by the importer of the products and affect the pricing of goods. Steel, aluminum, lumber, and electrical components are just some of the examples of the wide variety of construction materials that can be affected by import taxes and experience price fluctuations.
